candidates.title: Assignment Matters: Early Exposure and Career Outcomes
candidates.name: Shaheen Naseer

candidates.title: Intergenerational Mobility and Long-Term Care
candidates.abstract: This paper investigates how long-term care risk facing grandparents impacts the intergenerational mobility of children in the United States. I first show that the long-term care needs of grandparents impact both time and monetary investments families make in children. Motivated by these data patterns, I develop and estimate an overlapping generations model in which parents and grandparents interact with limited commitment to make long-term care, childcare, saving, and human capital investment choices. I find that long-term care needs explain 12% of the intergenerational correlation in earnings. Policies that provide coverage for formal long-term care costs increase intergenerational mobility whereas policies that provide payments for informal caregivers decrease intergenerational mobility. These effects are driven by changes in the time and monetary investments families make in their children as a result of these policy changes.
candidates.name: Alexis Smith

candidates.title: Misspecification-Aware Sequential Social Learning
candidates.name: Ana Sofia Teixeira Teles

candidates.title: When Transparency Backfires: Expert Selection and Communication
candidates.name: Arslan Ali

candidates.title: Wedding Bells or School Bells: Constraints on Marriage Timing and Women’s Educational Investments.
candidates.abstract: In many developing countries, women marry young, and married women are far less likely to be enrolled in school than single women of the same age. This paper studies how the timing of marriage affects women’s educational attainment in India. I exploit variation in marriage timing generated by a common social practice in which daughters marry in birth order. Instrumental variables estimates imply that a one-year increase in age at marriage raises women’s probability of completing high school by 6.1 percentage points. I then develop and estimate a dynamic equilibrium model in which households choose schooling and marriage timing in a directed-search marriage market. Estimates imply that although grooms prefer younger brides, the value they place on women's education more than offsets the associated age penalty. Even so, the age penalty, schooling costs, a finite search horizon, and birth-order constraints limit the gains from postponing marriage, thereby sustaining early marriage in equilibrium. I use the estimated model to evaluate an increase in the minimum legal marriage age. The policy raises schooling primarily among high-income women but generates substantial welfare losses by worsening marriage prospects. These findings show the importance of household resources and marriage-market equilibrium responses for policies aimed at increasing women's education.
candidates.name: Asha Bharadwaj

candidates.title: Mental Health, Physical Health and Lifetime Earnings Inequality
candidates.abstract: How much do differences in mental and physical health contribute to lifetime earnings inequality? Using the UK Household Longitudinal Study, I document that mental and physical health have very different dynamics and that employment and earnings losses concentrate among individuals who are unhealthy on both dimensions at once. I then develop a structural lifecycle model of labor supply in which mental and physical health follow separate processes and affect earnings, the cost of working, and survival. Removing differences in mental health lowers the variance of log lifetime earnings between ages 25 and 55 by 26.2%, removing differences in physical health lowers it by 21.3%, and removing both lowers it by 32.6%. Mental health accounts for more of the joint effect than physical health, accounting for 18.8% of the total variance against 13.8% for physical health. Four of the sixteen composite health states, those unhealthy on both dimensions, account for the entire joint effect. A decomposition by channel shows that health matters for lifetime earnings almost entirely because it raises the cost of working, and not because it lowers pay or shortens lives.
candidates.name: Ben Boyajian

candidates.title: Probationary Periods: Incentivizing Effort and Facilitating Learning
candidates.name: Burak Arici

candidates.title: The Collapse of the Long Work Week
candidates.name: Cache Ellsworth

candidates.title: Enrollment, Targeting, and Labor Market Effects of Work Requirements: Evidence from SNAP
candidates.abstract: Work requirements in U.S. safety net programs are often presented as a way to encourage work and screen less-needy participants off the program. This paper studies the participation, targeting, labor, and welfare effects of work requirements in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) for able-bodied adults without dependents (ABAWDs). Using administrative data from Virginia and quasi-experimental variation in county-level waivers from SNAP work requirements, I show that waivers increase ABAWD SNAP participation by 21.1%. Work requirement waivers improve the targeting efficiency of SNAP by increasing enrollment for more disadvantaged ABAWDs and by increasing participation among older and disabled adults living with ABAWDs. Turning to labor market outcomes, I show that work requirement waivers have no impact on earnings or employment. Using these empirical results I discuss implied welfare effects of work requirements. This paper has implications for recent expansions of work requirements in SNAP and Medicaid from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
candidates.name: Caitlin Dutta

candidates.title: Asymmetric Information and Search Frictions in Auto Loans
candidates.name: Davi Doneda Mittelstadt

candidates.title: The Policy Duet: Coordination in U.S. Monetary–Fiscal Communication
candidates.abstract: This paper studies the macroeconomic effects of communication coordination about inflation between U.S. monetary and fiscal authorities. I construct a novel dataset of approximately 250,000 speeches, statements, and other policy documents from the Federal Reserve, the Treasury, the White House, and Congress spanning 1911–2025. I use this corpus to build a communication coordination index (CCI) that captures the extent to which monetary and fiscal authorities send aligned or divergent messages about inflation. To identify the causal effects of communication coordination, I exploit variation in the political proximity between FOMC members and the congressional majority, drawing on the Fed's formal accountability to Congress. Using a vector autoregression identified with this instrumental variable, I find that a positive communication coordination shock has sizable expansionary effects: output rises immediately, unemployment falls, and hours worked, inflation, and interest rates increase. The joint rise in output and inflation indicates that the shock propagates like a demand shock, with the interest rate response reflecting a Taylor-rule-type policy reaction. Counterfactual analysis identifies the decline in real economic uncertainty as the dominant transmission mechanism. A New Keynesian model with asymmetric information, in which monetary and fiscal authorities communicate through distinct noisy signals, rationalizes these findings. Higher coordination improves households' inference about future economic conditions, lowers their uncertainty, and stimulates aggregate demand through reduced precautionary saving.
candidates.name: Dogukan GUNEY

candidates.title: The 1980s Recession and US Labor Market Inequality
candidates.abstract: Almost 60% of the drastic rise in 90–10 wage inequality since 1979 happened in the five-year period between 1980–1985, shortly after the twin recessions of the 1980s. This paper studies the contribution of this recession to the abrupt transformation of the wage distribution over this period. Using longitudinal linked employer-employee records for 5.3 million workers, we exploit variation in exposure to the recession across local labor markets to estimate the effects on worker’s labor market trajectories. We find that the recession persistently reduced earnings and employment, with the largest effects for workers at the bottom of the earnings distribution. The recession persistently reduced local labor market demand in these places, with a fifth of the recession’s unemployment shock still present a decade later. It also substantially weakened unions, extrapolating our estimates suggests that it can account for 42 percent of the national decline in union density over the decade. To understand the aggregate consequences of the recession, we construct counterfactual wage distributions under a less severe recession. Our estimates imply that the rise in wage dispersion between 1979 and 1988 would have been up to 20 percent smaller under the less severe counterfactual and that 35–40 percent of the recession’s effect on wage inequality is accounted for by its effects on unions. Our results suggest that the post-1980s rise in wage inequality was not purely the product of secular forces and that the recession meaningfully contributed to this rise by reshaping labor market institutions in the US.
candidates.name: Donato (Danny) Onorato

candidates.title: Labor Inspections, Misallocation, and Welfare
candidates.abstract: This paper studies the aggregate effects of labor regulations when enforcement is endogenous. Labor regulations impose costs on firms, but can be corrective when labor markets are imperfectly competitive. When enforcement occurs through worker complaints, regulations bind more tightly at larger, more productive firms – simultaneously expanding employment and taxing growth, leaving the net effect ambiguous. We embed a model of worker complaints and firm compliance in a general-equilibrium, imperfectly competitive labor market with an informal sector. We use a novel dataset from Peru’s labor inspection agency to estimate the complaint and inspection process by maximum likelihood, recovering the remaining parameters by simulated method of moments. We find that enforcement attracts workers to formal firms, which, surprisingly, pushes compliance down and improves both allocation of labor and total surplus relative to no enforcement. Perfect enforcement of these regulations, however, would reduce welfare dramatically. An analysis of labor regulations that focuses only on their costs overstates their welfare loss and misses their interaction with existing misallocation.
candidates.name: Eshaan Patel

candidates.title: Borrowing to do, doing to learn
candidates.abstract: This paper examines how learning by doing interacts with financial frictions and explores the quantitative consequences of this interplay for firm growth and allocative efficiency. I build a heterogeneous-firm model in which productivity accumulates through input use and where firms face borrowing limits. I calibrate the model to match new estimates of the elasticity of future revenue-based productivity (TFPR) to current input use from Spanish and Portuguese firm-level data. From the calibrated model, I find that the elasticity of future physical productivity (TFP) to current input use is 0.09. I then show that output losses from financial frictions are 50% larger with learning by doing. This amplification arises because allocative efficiency losses are twice as large, and because financial frictions directly lower productivity in constrained firms by 4% on average. Furthermore, I show that a planner that ignores learning by doing can recover only 10% of productivity losses from misallocation in the long run and worsens allocative efficiency in the short run.
candidates.name: Eugenio Gonzalez Flores

candidates.title: Rational Search with Learning
candidates.name: Fung Ngai

candidates.title: Effort Choices and Funding Instruments in Higher Education
candidates.abstract: This paper examines the effects of Free College policies on student enrollment and academic performance, with a focus on the 2016 Chilean reform that granted tuition-free higher education to students from the lowest five income deciles. Using a difference-in-differences approach, we find that Free College increased enrollment and persistence in higher education but had modest effects on graduation and dropout rates. To disentangle the role of student effort from selection effects, we develop a structural model in which students choose effort levels in response to financial incentives. Our results highlight that Free College expanded access, in particular for low-achieving students. Despite the removal of academic progress requirements, we found no evidence of weakening performance.
candidates.name: Guillem FOUCAULT I LLOPART

candidates.title: The Wisconsin Guarantee: A Top Percent Policy’s Impact on Flagship Access
candidates.abstract: Policies that guarantee admission to the flagship university for the highest performing students from every high school in the state have the potential to make enrollment more proportionally representative of the state’s high schools. However, existing evidence shows that these policies have only a modest impact on high school to flagship enrollment patterns. It is unclear whether these policies fail to induce new applications, fail to alter admissions decisions, or both. This paper studies the effects of Wisconsin’s new top percent policy at the state flagship, UW–Madison, where students in the top five percent of their high school class are now guaranteed admission. Using a difference-in-differences design comparing Wisconsin and Minnesota high school graduates, I find that the policy increased the probability a student from Wisconsin applied to UW–Madison by only 0.4 percentage points, equivalent to roughly 240 additional applications annually. Students also respond to the policy’s early action requirement by shifting when they submit applications. I then estimate whether guarantee-eligible applicants would have been admitted under the university’s preexisting admissions process and predict that 95 percent would have likely been admitted without the guarantee. I find little change in the distribution of UW–Madison’s in-state freshmen enrolling from the state’s various high schools. My findings provide evidence that top percent policies may not meaningfully change enrollment patterns when they have limited impact on students’ application choices and when guarantee-eligible applicants would have likely otherwise been admitted. This highlights a limitation of admission guarantees alone and suggests that efforts to change enrollment patterns may also need to target students’ application choices.
candidates.name: Heather Little

candidates.title: When Health Insurance Extends Beyond Health: Postpartum Medicaid and Household Spending
candidates.abstract: We study how extending coverage of Medicaid can impact household spending and resource reallocation. The Families First Coronavirus Response Act (FFCRA), temporarily mandated continuous Medicaid enrollment during the COVID-19 public health emergency, which effectively extended coverage for all women enrolled in Medicaid during pregnancy. Using monthly product-level purchase records from the NielsenIQ Consumer Panel (2019–2020), linked to state-specific Medicaid income thresholds, we analyze how spending patterns of households with newborns responded to FFCRA. Difference-in-differences estimates show that extended postpartum coverage roughly doubled spending on baby care products and increased total household expenditures by about 21 percent. The increase in spending occurs after 60 days postpartum, providing evidence that coverage extension acted as an expansion to the budget constraint. Further, we find that the increase in household resources translates to an increase in healthcare utilization using data from the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring Survey (PRAMS). Taken together, the results show how a major public insurance program can shape household resource allocation beyond healthcare use alone.
candidates.name: Hexuan Li

candidates.title: Who Gains from Maternal Employment? Self-Employment, Childcare, and Child Development
candidates.abstract: Whether a mother's employment helps or harms her child depends on how well formal childcare substitutes for her time. I estimate a household life-cycle model of work arrangements, time, and child skill formation on UK panel data, and find that this substitutability differs sharply by education. Using the paid-versus-self-employment margin, I decompose a work arrangement into three attributes: flexibility, earnings level, and earnings volatility. Fathers' time responds little to a young child, so mothers are the sole margin of adjustment. A college-educated mother's time is her child's most productive input, which formal care substitutes for poorly, while for a non-college mother it substitutes well. Full-time employment therefore lowers a child's skills by 0.15–0.22 SD when the mother is college educated but raises them by 0.12–0.16 SD when she is not. Flexible hours without a pay penalty raise maternal employment by up to 4 percentage points but leave child skills essentially unchanged, because mothers take the added hours from leisure rather than time with the child. Childcare raises skills only when tagged by education. Pairing the two policies benefits both groups and raises the projected lifetime earnings of children of non-college mothers by up to 6 percent.
candidates.name: Hyun Soo Suh

candidates.title: Piece by Piece, Hour by Hour: Wage-Setting, Productivity, and Turnover
candidates.abstract: The choice of compensation method is known to affect employees’ effort levels, their selection into employment, and their human capital accumulation. However, in settings with especially high turnover, the costs of replacing employees can become significant and affect firm production. We explore whether a change in compensation scheme that leaves mean wages unchanged can nevertheless affect productivity and turnover using a quasi-experimental staggered adoption of new pay for truck drivers at a large American motor carrier firm. We demonstrate that, when drivers’ mileage pay is augmented with hourly pay for non-driving tasks, they reduce driving hours by less than an hour while increasing on-duty time by one hour. While mean weekly wages do not significantly change, we observe a 6% decline in paid mileage and a 23-35% reduction in the probability of quitting in a given week when drivers receive both mileage and hourly pay. We explore possible mechanisms for these results, such as changes in the volatility of pay, the average speed drivers travel, or the modification “formed habits” around their expectations of weekly pay.
candidates.name: Jared Grogan

candidates.title: Price Discrimination in Electric Vehicle Fast Charging
candidates.name: John Higgins

candidates.title: Beyond the Label: Do Ecodesign Regulations Reduce Real-World Energy Use?
candidates.name: Kai Gao

candidates.title: Fenced Off: Export Processing Zones and the Local Economy in China
candidates.name: Kai Gu

candidates.title: Skin Tone and Racial Inequality in the US: Evidence from the 20th Century
candidates.abstract: Empirical work on racial inequality typically relies on a binary Black–white comparison, treating racial categories as uniform and masking meaningful variation in how individuals are treated within groups. Using newly collected WWII draft registration records containing information on skin tone for the near universe of men born between 1898–1929, linked to the 1940 Census, we document large intra-racial disparities by skin color. Black men with dark skin earn about 37% less than their lighter-skinned peers. This unconditional gap is economically significant—if all Black men earned what light-skinned Black men did, the Black–white earnings gap in 1940 would be roughly 19% smaller. We explore several mechanisms behind these disparities. Comparing brothers raised in the same household, family fixed effects eliminate the entire education gap, yet darker-skinned brothers still earn 8% less (8 log points)—roughly a quarter of the unconditional gap—pointing to a labor market penalty distinct from the categorical disadvantages tied to racial classification. We then consider the role of discriminatory institutions. While Jim Crow exposure depresses educational attainment for Black men overall, we find no differential impact by skin tone, consistent with the one drop rule. Finally, exploiting WWII-driven variation in labor market tightness, we find that shocks that reduced Black–white inequality did not necessarily narrow intra-racial skin tone differences. Our results show that skin tone inequality reflects both inherited disadvantage and distinct discriminatory forces that sort Black men along color lines and likely different than those driving broader racial inequality.
candidates.name: Kamelia Stavreva

candidates.title: Biopharma firms with negative enterprise value
candidates.abstract: “Enterprise Value” of a public company is the difference between its market capitalization and net cash. When a biopharma firm announces negative trial results, its stock price plummets, and its market cap can drop below its net cash balance, implying a negative enterprise value. While roughly 100 US biopharma firms went public in 2020, half of them ended up with negative enterprise value due to scientific failures. Motivated by this empirical observation, this paper investigates the cause of the negative enterprise value puzzle and further examines whether the biopharma boom during the pandemic was fundamentally justified. The first part of the paper uses manually collected data to document the performance of biopharma firms that went public. The descriptive analysis shows evidence of inefficient continuation due to agency conflicts and suggests that investors might have provided too much capital at the time of IPO. To study whether venture capital investors would have behaved differently with the possibility of staging capital injection over time, the second part of the paper uses the equilibrium model of VC financing developed by Parry (2025) to solve for the optimal contract (upfront or staged financing) that trades off the cost of inefficient continuation against the risk of early termination. Preliminary results show that upfront financing is indeed preferred, since the underlying project characteristics of biopharma firms imply large value loss from early termination.
candidates.name: Lin FANG

candidates.title: The Distributional Welfare Effects of Labour Market Power
candidates.abstract: Labour market power— firms marking down wages below workers’ marginal product of labour— has aggregate welfare costs. But how are these costs distributed across members of a society? Labour market power generates winners and losers, as wage markdowns shift revenue toward firm owners at workers’ expense. Yet gains and losses across these groups are not clear cut. Markdowns are heterogeneous across firms, households earn both labour and capital income, and efficiency losses may be large enough to make everyone worse off. I measure the distributional welfare effects of labour market power in Canada using a second-order accurate approximation of how welfare changes following the elimination of labour market power in the economy. I combine this approximation with a structural model of labour market power, and take it to administrative Canadian data. I find that the incidence of labour market power falls mainly on those in the top income quartile, with the upper-middle class facing the greatest net cost and the top percentile of income earners gaining the greatest net benefit.
candidates.name: Madeline Hanson

candidates.title: Estate Taxes, Parental Transfers and Inequality
candidates.abstract: Estate taxes incentivize parental substitution away from bequests and towards inter vivos transfers. This distortion in the timing of giving renders the effect of estate taxation on intergenerational mobility ambiguous: when parents and children face different returns, shifting resources earlier in the life cycle may change children's wealth accumulation before inheritances are received. I formalize this mechanism in a simple model of one-sided altruism with inter vivos transfers, bequests, estate taxes and heterogeneous returns. The effect of changes in estate taxation depend upon three key elasticities: parental inter vivos transfers and bequests, and children's consumption. Empirically, I construct a database of state-level estate tax exemptions for 46 states from 1991 to 2019 and exploit variation in these exemptions to estimate parental giving responses. I then bring these estimates to a quantitative model to evaluate the effects of estate taxation on intergenerational wealth mobility.
candidates.name: Marlena Eley

candidates.title: The Criminal Justice League: Evaluating Multidisciplinary Approaches to Combating Intimate Partner Violence
candidates.name: Mary Daniels

candidates.title: Product-Harm Crises and Intermediaries in the Used Car Market
candidates.name: Masahiro Nishida

candidates.title: Sorting Over Wildfire Risk Information
candidates.name: Michael Fogarty

candidates.title: Judge IV Designs with Multiple Treatments and Instruments
candidates.name: Myunghyun Song

candidates.title: On the Value of Sales Quotas
candidates.name: NATHAN HATTERSLEY

candidates.title: Housing Market Segmentation and Monetary Policy
candidates.abstract: Recent evidence shows that contractionary monetary policy raises U.S. housing rents even as house prices fall. I argue that this response reflects a shift in housing demand toward renting in segmented markets: tighter credit raises the cost of owning for constrained households, and because converting housing to rental use is costly, rental supply cannot expand enough to absorb the added demand, so rents rise. I quantify this mechanism in a New Keynesian model estimated on 1975–2019 U.S. data and disciplined jointly by the rent response to monetary policy and the slope of the tenure-supply curve. Tightening monetary policy in response to rising rents can reinforce the shift toward renting, and thus rental pressure. Excluding shelter from the target improves welfare, and a re-optimized rule with a much stronger response to goods inflation improves it further. Additional responses to rents or house prices add little.
candidates.name: Pablo De Llanos

candidates.title: Spillovers Under Common Shocks In Panel Data: Estimation and Inference
candidates.name: Qiyang Yu

candidates.title: Priced Out: Financing Frictions and Startup Mortality
candidates.abstract: Startups raise capital in a sequence of rounds, and each round exposes them to financing risk, the possibility that a viable firm fails because it cannot raise its next round on acceptable terms. This paper asks how much startup failure financing risk causes, and what determines it. We develop a dynamic model of staged equity financing in which a firm with stochastic fundamentals must repeatedly return to the market to raise more capital, and we summarize financing frictions as a wedge between the price of outside capital and its frictionless level. Two results organize the analysis. First, because equity is repriced at every round, repricing substitutes for coordination among investors, so the equilibrium is unique and staged equity does not admit self-fulfilling failure. Second, a firm fails when its fundamentals fall below the level at which investors are willing to fund another round, and the wedge raises that level: firms that would survive in a frictionless market fail instead. We estimate the model by simulated method of moments on a panel of venture-backed firms from PitchBook. A counterfactual that removes the wedge then measures the share of observed startup failures attributable to financing frictions rather than to fundamentals.
candidates.name: Rodrigo Pacheco

candidates.title: Dangerous Talk
candidates.name: Rodrigo Yañez Naudon

candidates.title: Soft Skills, Hard Times: Why New College Graduates Are Falling Behind
candidates.abstract: The labor market outcomes for young college graduates have been worsening since the Great Recession. We document that this secular trend coincides with a rise in demand for soft skills by employers. We propose that this shift in skill demand disproportionately affects young workers, who have had less opportunity to accumulate these skills through on-the-job experience. To quantify this mechanism, we build a general equilibrium search model with heterogeneous agents and on-the-job skill accumulation, calibrated to the US labor market. A rise in demand for soft skills explains about one-third of the increase in the unemployment rate of young college graduates in this model.
candidates.name: SURYANSH UPMANYU

candidates.title: Who Bears Firm Risk? Employment Contracts, Firm Uncertainty, and Differential Risk Sharing
candidates.abstract: This paper studies how firm uncertainty shapes the choice between permanent and temporary contracts, the allocation of risk between firms and workers, and the design of employment protection. Using French administrative data, I document that temporary workers are doubly exposed to firm risk. They are more likely to work at firms facing greater uncertainty, and their wage growth and separations respond 2.4 and 4 times as strongly to firm productivity shocks as those of permanent workers. I develop and structurally estimate a dynamic search model with firm competition and risk-sharing contracts under two-sided limited commitment. Firing costs act as a commitment device, allowing permanent contracts to provide greater insurance but also to sustain unprofitable matches. Temporary contracts provide less insurance but allow costless separation. In the estimated model, greater firm uncertainty favors temporary contracts, and higher worker skill favors permanent ones. I then ask what a uniform employment protection policy implies when firms differ in risk. Removing firing costs on permanent contracts generates opposite responses across firms: employment and output rise at stable firms and fall at uncertain ones, and aggregate effects mask this heterogeneity. Worker welfare falls and firm values rise, with both effects largest at the most uncertain firms.
candidates.name: Sabrina Ben Said

candidates.title: Who Pays Attention? Firm Size, Information, and Monetary-Non-Neutrality
candidates.abstract: A large literature that microfounds information frictions as a source of monetary non-neutrality emphasizes average firm attention to monetary shocks–summarized by the average Kalman gain, or the weight firms place on new information–as the key statistic governing the degree of monetary non-neutrality. I use an LLM to construct a measure of inflation attention from firms’ 10-K filings and apply a state-space model to recover the implied Kalman gains. I find that this attention is systematically related to firm size, with larger firms being more attentive. I develop a model of heterogeneous firms and endogenous information acquisition that rationalizes this gradient. Firm size is a first-order determinant of the profit loss from mispricing and therefore of the incentive to acquire information. I then show that when firm size is also systematically related to firms’ pricing behavior, their partial-equilibrium cost pass-through, the allocation of attention across firms matters for aggregate price rigidity. In the empirically relevant case in which larger firms have lower cost pass-through, the negative covariance between attention and cost pass-through increases aggregate price rigidity. Aggregate price rigidity is governed by a small set of firm-level steady-state objects: firm size, cost pass-through, demand elasticity, and the Kalman gain. Using empirical measures of these objects, I find that the implied Phillips curve is about 40% flatter than under a symmetric firm-homogeneous attention benchmark. I calibrate the structural model to the U.S. economy in the 2010s and obtain a flattening of similar magnitude. Finally, I conduct a counterfactual in which I shift the productivity distribution to restore top-firm concentration to its 1990 level, allowing information acquisition to adjust endogenously. I show that changes in market structure can have substantially different effects on monetary non-neutrality once the allocation of attention is allowed to respond.
candidates.name: Sanhitha Jugulum

candidates.title: Middle (Mostly) Matters More: The Dynamic Effects of School Quality on Longer-Run Outcomes
candidates.abstract: I estimate grade-specific measures of school quality using test scores and evaluate their effects on high school graduation, college attendance and completion, and earnings. Raising school quality - especially in middle and high school - boosts early career earnings and improves college enrollment and completion outcomes, excepting two-year college participation. There are interactions between vintages of school quality – attending a good high school is more beneficial when preceded by attending a high quality middle school. The returns to raising school quality are pronounced for low-skill students. These results suggest that constrained schools could improve outcomes by targeting resources towards low-skill middle-school students.
candidates.name: Sharada Dharmasankar

candidates.title: Managerial Experience, Firm Size, and Economic Development: Evidence from Japan's Decolonization
candidates.abstract: I study how the scarcity of workers with managerial experience limits firm size and economic development, combining evidence from a natural experiment with a quantitative model. After World War II, three million Japanese civilians, many of them with managerial experience, were forced to return to Japan. I use repatriates’ historical family ties to Japanese districts to isolate exogenous variation in local inflows of workers with managerial experience. The inflow shifted employment from self-employment toward wage work and from agriculture toward manufacturing and services. Firms grew larger, expanded beyond their headquarters cities, and participated more in overseas programs teaching modern U.S. management practices. I develop a spatial model in which managerial experience expands the pool of workers qualified for management. Managers supervise production within establishments and implement practices that raise productivity across the firm’s establishment network. Removing the managerial experience of these repatriates lowers aggregate output per worker by 4 percent. Firms’ geographic expansion accounts for about a quarter of this effect, amplifying the aggregate impact from managerial experience.
candidates.name: Shizuka Inoue

candidates.title: Foreign Language and Social Preferences
candidates.name: Simon Li

candidates.title: Inclusionary Zoning and Access to Opportunity: Evidence from Washington, D.C.
candidates.name: So Young Kim

candidates.title: Geoeconomic Pressure, Sovereign Risk, and Asset Prices: Evidence from Mexico
candidates.abstract: A powerful country can raise a smaller sovereign’s borrowing costs without imposing a single tariff or sanction, simply by threatening to, repricing its default risk well before any of that risk is realized. I study this channel using the pressure that Donald Trump directed at Mexico during his 2016 campaign and first year in office, a setting that isolates the geoeconomic shock from Mexico’s own fiscal position. Using a synthetic-control estimator on daily credit default swap data, I find that this pressure raised Mexico’s sovereign spread by 24 basis points on average. A textual analysis of Trump’s socialmedia posts corroborates this interpretation: the spread responds to his threats, more to trade threats than migration threats. I then trace how this Mexico-specific repricing transmits to asset prices: a one-basis-point increase in the spread depreciates the peso by 5.3 cents and lowers Mexican equity returns by 0.11 percent, with financial and tradablegoods sectors most exposed. A quantitative sovereign-default model, in which the pressure tilts the income process toward adverse states, rationalizes the repricing as the price of a genuine shift toward adverse income states and implies a welfare cost of 0.02 percent of lifetime consumption for the transitory episode, and an average consumption contraction of 0.13 percent. As complementary, higher-frequency evidence that avoids time aggregation, filtering and sufficient-statistic methods put the consumption drop at 0.35 percent.
candidates.name: Stefano Lord Medrano

candidates.title: A Network Theory of Project Management
candidates.name: Steve Yeh

candidates.title: The Effects of County-Level Naloxone Distribution on Drug Usage and Health Outcomes: Evidence from Indiana
candidates.name: Stroud Payne

candidates.title: Barriers to industrial growth and long-run productive efficiency: the role of policy-induced misallocation (with Abhishek Deshwal)
candidates.abstract: We study how government-created distortions in upstream coal markets affect long-run productivity growth in India’s electricity industry. The government coal monopoly administratively allocates subsidized coal primarily to inefficient state-owned plants while forcing efficient private generators to purchase coal at market prices often 1.5-2 times higher. This unequal access distorts not only the allocation of electricity production today, but also incentives to invest in new generating capacity. Using plant-level data for 2006-2017 and detailed administrative records of coal supply contracts, we estimate a dynamic oligopoly model of capacity investment for coal-fired generators. We use the estimated model to quantify how eliminating distortions would change investment and the long-run productivity of the electricity sector.
candidates.name: Tianyu Luo

candidates.title: Computerization and the Rising Return to Long-Hour Jobs
candidates.abstract: Occupations differ substantially in their average weekly hours worked. I show that, from 1975 to 2007, hourly wages increased much more in long-hours occupations while average hours by occupation remained stable. This differential wage growth accounts for an important share of the rise in earnings inequality over this period. To understand these patterns, I develop a labor market model in which occupational differences arise from the cost of handing work off between workers: when handoffs are costly, firms offer compensation schedules that reward long workweeks. I provide novel survey evidence supporting this mechanism. I further show that in occupations with high handoff costs workers are less substitutable with computer capital, consistent with the notion that tacit knowledge shapes both worker–worker and worker–capital substitutability. In the model, a decline in computer prices raises relative wages in high-handoff cost (long-hour) occupations. The model calibrated to 1975–1980 labor market data reproduces 81 percent of the observed increase in the hours–wage covariance following an externally disciplined decline in computer prices. Counterfactual improvements in handoff technology shorten workweeks and reduce earnings inequality, quantifying the potential distributional effects of organizational reform that makes workers better substitutes for one another.

candidates.title: Wealth Inequality and Sudden Stops
candidates.abstract: This paper documents that countries with greater wealth inequality experience deeper recessions during sudden stops. Household-level data show that more unequal countries have a higher share of indebted households, whose debt and assets decrease during sudden stops. In a model with heterogeneous households subject to borrowing constraints, I analytically characterize that greater inequality increases the fraction of constrained households, amplifying declines in asset prices and consumption following an adverse aggregate shock. Quantitatively, a 0.01 increase in the wealth Gini amplifies the declines in GDP and consumption by 0.07 and 0.11 percentage points, respectively, per percentage point of capital outflow during a sudden stop. Wealth taxation, when optimally combined with capital control on external debt, limits the increase in constrained households during sudden stops by reducing households’ borrowing needs through transfers, whereas the increase remains substantial under optimal capital control alone.

candidates.title: Peer Earnings Disclosure at Work: Evidence from Two Field Experiments
candidates.abstract: I study how recurring peer earnings disclosure affects labor supply in performance-based work using two large-scale field experiments with over 3,000 ride-hailing drivers. During each six-week intervention, all drivers received twice-weekly updates on their own cumulative earnings; I randomized whether these updates also reported the average earnings of their reference group of ten similar drivers. An incentivized measure of drivers’ demand for peer earnings information, elicited at baseline, identifies the same responsive worker type in both experiments nearly one year apart. The labor-supply response to peer information, however, reverses: information-seeking drivers increase platform hours by 6% in the first experiment but reduce them by 5% in the second, when platform earning opportunities are weaker. Non-information-seeking drivers show no detectable response in either experiment. By contrast, both types respond similarly to randomized monetary incentives. Beyond relative-pay concerns, peer earnings may convey information about earning opportunities. I develop a conceptual framework distinguishing learning about shared market conditions from learning about the returns to alternative work strategies. Consistent with market learning, peer-information effects become more positive following favorable market surprises, but show little relationship with predictable conditions. The findings show that information demand predicts who responds to peer earnings disclosure, while learning about shared earning opportunities helps explain how they respond.
